title: Why Open Minds Can Still Split Into Two Camps

source.title: Opinion Dynamics and Bounded Confidence: Models, Analysis, and Simulation
source.venue: Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS) vol. 5, no. 3

intro.summary: The paper asks when a group of people who keep adjusting their opinions to each other ends up agreeing, splitting into two camps, or breaking into many small groups. It first reviews older models in which everyone averages everyone else's opinion, which usually leads to agreement. It then studies a model of 'bounded confidence', in which people only listen to others whose opinions are already close to their own, using some mathematical proofs and many computer simulations. The main finding is that as people's open-mindedness grows, the group does not drift smoothly toward agreement: it passes through distinct phases, from many opinions, to two camps, to consensus. The two camps form because people at the edges are pulled only toward the middle. The main limitations are that these are idealised models: opinions are a single number, everyone can hear everyone, and the results come from simulations and proofs, not from data on real people. This lesson does not cover the Friedkin–Johnsen model of stubborn agents, the model in which weights change over time, or the paper's work on lopsided confidence, including the case where people listen more to their own side. These, along with the paper's early finding that local neighbourhoods may prevent polarisation, are good topics to study next.
background: An opinion here is a number on a line, for example an estimate between 0 and 1, so that 'closer' and 'further apart' have a clear meaning.
A weighted average is an average where some values count more than others, like a final grade where the exam counts more than the homework.
A model that repeats the same rule round after round is called a dynamical system, and the question is where it settles in the end.
When a rule's own inputs decide whom it listens to, small differences can change the outcome sharply; mathematicians call such a rule nonlinear.
intro.aha: Making everyone a bit more open-minded does not bring a group steadily closer to agreement: at medium open-mindedness the group reliably splits into two camps, because the people at the edges are pulled only inward and drag the middle apart.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Picture a group of experts trying to agree on one estimate, or a whole society talking about an issue. Each person listens to others and nudges their own view. Sometimes this ends in agreement, sometimes in two opposed camps, sometimes in many scattered groups. The paper asks what decides which of these happens.
primer.quote: When does opinion formation within an interacting group lead to consensus, polarization or fragmentation?

primer.heading: The older answer: averaging leads to agreement
primer.body: Earlier models assumed that each person replaces their opinion with a weighted average of everyone's opinions, round after round. Under fairly mild conditions this always ends in consensus. That left a puzzle that researchers had already noticed: real communities often split in two, yet these models kept predicting agreement.
primer.quote: Since universal ultimate agree-ment is an ubiquitous outcome of a very broad class of mathematical models, we are naturally led to inquire what on earth one must a ssume in order to generate th e bimodal outcome of community cleavage studies.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: The authors added one realistic twist: each person only takes seriously those whose opinions lie within a set distance of their own. This distance is called the confidence level. Because whom you listen to now depends on what everyone currently thinks, the maths becomes much harder. The authors proved some general results, then ran many computer simulations. In each one, 625 random opinions update at the same moment, round after round, at many different confidence levels.
primer.quote: We will randomly generate a start distribution of 625 opinions. Updating is simultaneous.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: With tiny confidence, many separate opinions survive. In one example run with a confidence of 0.01, exactly 38 opinions remained. With medium confidence (0.15 in one run), the group ends in two camps. With large confidence (0.25), everyone agrees. The camps form because people at the extremes have others on only one side, so they are pulled toward the centre and bunch up. Once two groups drift out of each other's reach, they never interact again.
primer.quote: As the homogeneous and symmetric confidence interval increases we transit from phase to phase. More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity).

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The work shows that two camps can form even when nobody is stubborn or hostile, simply because people ignore views that are too far from their own. It also argues that computer simulation is needed when rules are nonlinear, because proofs become hard to find. The opinions are single numbers and everyone can in principle hear everyone, so the results describe a teaching world, not measured societies. Early simulations reported at the end suggest that talking only to neighbours may remove the two-camp phase altogether.
primer.quote: At least under bounded confidence locality of interactions may prevent societies from sharp polarisation.

concepts.title: Averaging round after round pulls opinions together
concepts.idea: If each person repeatedly replaces their opinion with a weighted average of their own and others' opinions, the gap between them shrinks every round until they agree.

predict.question: New case: Ana never listens to Ben. She keeps 100% of her own view, starting at 20. Ben keeps half of his own view (starting at 80) and takes half from Ana. What happens over many rounds?
options: They never agree, because Ana refuses to budge
They agree, at Ana's opinion of 20
They agree in the middle, at 50
Ben swings past Ana and ends up below 20
why: Tempting, because full stubbornness froze the lines in the model. But that needed both people to ignore each other. Here Ben still listens to Ana, so the gap halves every round.

Correct. Ana stays at 20 and Ben moves halfway to her each round: 50, 35, 27.5 and so on. The gap shrinks toward zero at Ana's opinion. In the paper's terms, both people give positive weight to the same person (Ana), so consensus is approached.
The meeting point was 50 in the model only because both people listened to each other equally. Here all the pull comes from Ana, so the shared opinion ends up where she stands.
Taking half from Ana puts Ben exactly halfway between himself and her. That point is always above 20, so he gets closer every round but never passes her.

terms.means: The share of your new opinion that comes from your own current opinion; the rest comes from others
Opinions getting closer and closer to one shared value, round after round
The paper's name for repeated averaging where everyone's weights stay fixed over time (studied by De Groot and Lehrer)

model.title: Two people averaging their views, round after round
model.note: Teaching model: only two people. Both keep the same fixed share of their own view, they start at 20 and 80 on a 0–100 scale, and both update at the same moment in whole rounds. This is the paper's fixed-weights averaging rule (eq. 2.1) with two agents. The paper allows any number of agents and unequal weights. The numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Share of their own view each person keeps

outputs.label: Share of the gap left after each round

steps.say: Meet Ana. Her opinion is on a 0–100 scale, say how good a new film is. She starts at 20.
Meet Ben. He starts far away, at 80. Each step to the right is one round of talking.
Each round, both of them blend their own view with the other's. This slider sets how much of their own view each one keeps. Watch the lines stretch out as it rises.
This box shows how much of the gap between them is left after each round.
These two boxes tell you how far apart they still are at rounds 5 and 10.

explore.prompt: Play with how much each person holds on to their own view. Can you make them agree fast without making them push-overs? Then can you make them close in slowly?

goals.text: Get Ana and Ben within 1 point of each other by round 5, while each still keeps more of their own view than they take from the other
hints: Should each person keep more of their own view, or less, to close the gap faster?
Each round the gap is multiplied by the share in the first box. By round 5 that has happened five times, and 60 times that result must fall below 1.
Lower the slider one notch at a time from where it starts. Stop before you reach an even split, because an even split breaks the 'keeps more of their own view' rule.

goals.text: Make them close in slowly: after 10 rounds they should still be more than 5 points apart, but less than 10
hints: Slower agreement means each person holds on to their own view more strongly.
Raise the slider one notch at a time and watch the 'Gap after 10 rounds' box.
The setting you want sits one notch below the one where they are still about 21 points apart.

feedback.correct: Right. Agreement does not need both people to move. It is enough that everyone gives some weight to a common person. Ben keeps moving toward a fixed Ana, so the gap halves each round and they meet at her opinion.
feedback.incorrect: You may have carried over the frozen lines from full stubbornness. Those needed both people to ignore each other. Here Ben still takes half his view from Ana, so each round he gets halfway closer to her. They meet at Ana's opinion, not in the middle.

steps.say: Each person keeps 80% of their own view and takes 20% of the other's. After round 1, Ana is at 0.8×20 + 0.2×80 = 32, and Ben is at 68.
The gap went from 60 to 36, so 60% of it survived. The 80% each keeps is called their self-weight. Every round the same share of the gap survives: 36, then about 22, then 13.
Now lower the self-weight so they listen to each other more. Only 20% of the gap survives each round, and by round 5 they are practically identical.
At an even split, each person takes exactly half from the other. Both jump to 50 in a single round.

Raise the self-weight high. Now 90% of the gap survives each round, and after 10 rounds they are still about 21 points apart. It is slower, but the lines still bend toward 50. This steady closing-in is called convergence.
Here is the one exception. If each keeps 100% of their own view, nobody listens, the gap never shrinks, and the lines stay flat at 20 and 80 forever.
So any listening at all, even a little, eventually pulls them together. Only total stubbornness stops it. With fixed weights like these, the paper calls this the classical model.

understand.explanation: Each round, every person's new opinion is a weighted average: part their own current view, part everyone else's. With two people who each keep the same self-weight, the gap between them is multiplied by the same share every round, so it shrinks steadily toward zero. Strictly, it approaches zero rather than hitting it, except at an even split. A high self-weight only slows this convergence down; only a self-weight of 100% stops it completely. The paper reviews this classical model (from De Groot and Lehrer) and states the result as a theorem: if any two people both give some weight to a common third person, the group approaches a consensus from any starting opinions. This is a mathematical result about the model with fixed weights, not an observation of real groups. Where the group ends up depends on the starting opinions and on who listens to whom.
understand.quote: A special case of Result 1 is given if every agent puts a positive weight on any other agent. This corresponds to the intuition that the group should approach a consensus if every agent takes the opinion of any other agent into account. On the other extreme is the case where every agent sticks to his opinion without taking care of any other opinion.

connect.caption: This is the paper's eq. 2.1 written for two agents. x_{1}(t) is Ana's opinion in round t and x_{2}(t) is Ben's. a_{11} is Ana's self-weight, set by the slider. a_{12} = 1 − a_{11} is the weight she gives Ben, and Ben uses the same weights in mirror image. Subtracting Ben's rule from Ana's shows that the gap is multiplied by a_{11} + a_{22} − 1 = 2w − 1 each round, which is the 'share of the gap left' box.

concepts.recap: Repeated averaging with fixed weights shrinks the gap by the same share every round, so any listening at all leads toward agreement; only total stubbornness prevents it.

concepts.title: Only listening to people who are already close
concepts.idea: Under bounded confidence, each person averages only the opinions within a distance ε of their own, so the set of people they listen to changes as opinions move.

predict.question: A new case. Mia holds 0.30 and Raj holds 0.50, so they are 0.20 apart. Mia listens up to 0.25 away, but Raj only listens up to 0.10 away. Both use the same rule: average everyone you hear, yourself included. Where are they after one round?
options: Mia moves to 0.40 and Raj stays at 0.50
Raj moves to 0.40 and Mia stays at 0.30
why: This assumes listening always goes both ways. Here each person checks the gap against their own range. The 0.20 gap is inside Mia's 0.25 but outside Raj's 0.10, so only Mia averages.
Correct. Mia hears herself and Raj, so she moves to (0.30 + 0.50) / 2 = 0.40. Raj hears only himself, so his average is his own 0.50 and he stays put.
This swaps the two people. The one with the wider range is the one who hears the other, and that is Mia, not Raj.
Disagreeing is not what blocks influence. What matters is whether the gap fits inside a person's range. It fits Mia's range, so Mia moves.

terms.means: How far away someone's opinion can be from yours and still be listened to: half the width of your listening window
The rule that you only take into account opinions within ε of your own and ignore everyone further away

model.title: Who you hear on the opinion line, and where that sends you next
model.note: Teaching model: one person's next step on an opinion line from 0 to 1. Five other people stay frozen in place, everyone shares one listening range, and everyone heard counts equally. This is the paper's bounded-confidence rule with a single shared ε. In the paper every opinion updates at the same time each round, and the simulations use up to 625 people. The positions here are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Six people sit on an opinion line from 0 to 1. You are the coloured dot at 0.40. Ana, Ben, Dev, Eli and Fay hold other views.
The shaded band around you shows how far you listen. Anyone inside it is heard. Anyone outside it is ignored.
This slider widens the band. Watch Dev slip inside it.
This slider moves your own opinion along the line.
The raised dot shows where you would move next: the plain average of everyone you hear, you included.

explore.prompt: Now steer it yourself. Each person counts only while they sit inside your band. Work out from the gaps who enters when, then check whether your next opinion lands where you expect.

goals.text: Stay at your starting opinion and hear exactly four people in all (you plus three others)
hints: A person enters the band when the range reaches their distance from you.
List the others by how far they are from 0.40. Dev is closest, then Ben.
The third-closest person is Eli. Widen the band until Eli is just inside but Ana is still outside.

goals.text: Hear at least two other people, yet barely move: your next move should be smaller than 0.005 either way
hints: You stay put when the pull from the left exactly balances the pull from the right.
Try hearing one person on each side and standing the same distance from both.
Ben and Dev make a good pair. Move to the point halfway between them, then widen the band just enough to reach both, but not Ana or Eli.

feedback.correct: Right. Each person checks the gap against their own range. Mia hears Raj and moves to the average, 0.40. Raj hears no one but himself and stays at 0.50. Who you hear depends only on distance and your range.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed that influence is mutual, or that disagreement blocks it. Under bounded confidence, each person counts the others whose opinions lie within their own ε. The 0.20 gap fits Mia's 0.25 range but not Raj's 0.10, so only Mia averages.

steps.say: Start narrow. The band holds only you, so People heard reads 1. Your next opinion is just your own, 0.40: you don't move.
Widen the band until it reaches Dev, 0.12 away. Now you average two opinions, 0.40 and 0.52, and your next opinion jumps right to 0.46.
Widen a little more and Ben, 0.18 away on the left, joins. With three voices the average swings back left, to 0.38.
This half-width has a name: the confidence level ε. Listening only to opinions within ε of your own is called bounded confidence.
Lower ε by just 0.01 and Ben drops out. You jump straight back to 0.46. One small notch removed a whole person, so the next step changes in a jump, not smoothly.
Now fix ε at 0.15 and move instead. Suppose you took your step to 0.46. Ben is now 0.24 away and out of range. Dev is still in.
Drift on to 0.55, and Eli, whom you ignored at the start, comes into range. Your circle changed only because your own opinion moved.
So who you listen to depends on what everyone currently thinks. In the paper all opinions move at once, so everyone's circle shifts every round.

understand.explanation: In the averaging model you just met, the weights people give each other stay fixed. Hegselmann and Krause change one thing. Each person gives equal weight to everyone whose opinion lies within ε of their own, themselves included, and gives zero weight to everyone else. Because opinions move each round, the set of people inside each window keeps changing too. Someone can enter or drop out, and the next step then jumps. That feedback, where opinions decide the weights and the weights move the opinions, makes the model nonlinear. The paper notes that this rules out the tidy matrix tools that work for the fixed-weight model, so it studies the model mainly by computer simulation.
understand.quote: Though elementary, the model is nonlinear in that the structure of the model changes with the states of the model given by the opinions of the agents

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence model (BC) with one shared ε. I(i, x) is the set of people inside your band. Its size |I| is People heard, and you are always in it. Your next opinion x_{i}(t+1) is the plain average of the opinions in that set. Your opinion x_{i} and the listening range ε decide who belongs to the set. The paper also allows each person their own ε_{i}.

concepts.recap: Under bounded confidence you average only the opinions within ε of yours. As opinions move, people enter and leave that window, so who influences whom keeps changing.

concepts.title: Once groups drift apart, they never reconnect
concepts.idea: When the gap between two neighbouring opinions grows beyond ε, nobody on one side is reachable through any chain of trust from the other side, so the two groups stop influencing each other forever.

terms.means: A gap wider than ε between two people who sit next to each other when everyone is lined up by opinion
A relay of listening: you listen to someone close to you, who listens to someone close to them, and so on
A group cut off by splits on both sides. Its members influence each other but nobody outside it
A gap that only one side can see across, because windows reach farther in one direction than the other

concepts.recap: A gap wider than ε between neighbours cuts every chain of confidence, and each side can then only average its own members, so the gap can never close again.

understand.explanation: Recall the rule from the last concept: each person averages only the opinions within distance ε of their own. Line everyone up by opinion. If two neighbours in that line end up more than ε apart, nobody below the gap listens to anyone above it, and nobody above listens to anyone below. The paper calls this a split. On each side, influence can still travel step by step, from you to someone close to you to someone close to them. That relay is a chain of confidence, but no chain crosses a split. So each side only ever averages its own members: the lower side's highest opinion cannot rise, the upper side's lowest cannot fall, and the gap cannot shrink back under ε. Each side becomes its own opinion world, a group whose members influence each other and nobody outside it. The paper states this as a basic property of the model when windows are equally wide on both sides. When windows reach farther in one direction, a one-sided split can close again. This is a property of the model's rules; real people may change whom they listen to for other reasons.
understand.quote: If a split between two agents occurs at some time it will remain a split forever.

activities.title: Five neighbours, one gap

steps.text: Five people rate a new town policy from 0 (hate it) to 1 (love it). Each listens only to opinions within ε = 0.2 of their own. Lined up, they are A = 0.10, B = 0.25, C = 0.40, D = 0.70 and E = 0.85.
Find who listens to whom. A and B are 0.15 apart, so they listen to each other. B and C are 0.15 apart, so they do too. A and C are 0.30 apart, so A does not listen to C directly.
steps.result: A → B → C is a chain of confidence: C's view reaches A through B

steps.text: Now look at C and D. They are 0.30 apart, more than ε. Everyone below C is even farther from D, and everyone above D is even farther from C.
steps.result: A split: no chain links {A, B, C} with {D, E}

steps.text: Round 1: everyone averages the opinions inside their window. A averages A and B: 0.175. B averages A, B and C: 0.25. C averages B and C: 0.325. D and E average each other: 0.775.

Check the gap. An average can never be bigger than the largest number in it. The lower group averages only its own members, so its top opinion can only stay put or fall. By the same logic, the upper group's bottom opinion can only stay put or rise.
Round 2: A, B and C are now all within 0.15 of each other, so each averages all three: 0.25. D and E stay at 0.775.
steps.result: Final: one camp at 0.25, one at 0.775

activities.takeaway: Once a gap wider than ε opens between neighbours, each side only averages itself. The gap can grow or stay the same, but it can never shrink, so {A, B, C} and {D, E} each become a separate opinion world.

activities.prompt: Six people with ε = 0.2. A line joins two people when their opinions are within 0.2 of each other, so they listen to each other. Select everyone in Ann's opinion world: Ann herself plus everyone her influence can reach through a chain of confidence.
hints: Ann listens directly only to Ben. Who does Ben listen to?
Keep following the lines until you hit a pair with no line between them.
Dee (0.50) and Eli (0.80) are 0.30 apart, which is more than ε.
activities.explanation: Ann does not listen to Cal or Dee directly, but influence relays along Ann–Ben–Cal–Dee, so all four share one opinion world. Dee and Eli are 0.30 apart, so there is a split between them. Everyone in Ann's group is even farther from Eli and Fay, so no chain crosses the gap. Eli and Fay form a second opinion world, and the two groups will never influence each other again.

activities.question: In the trace above, after a few rounds Ann's group has settled around 0.29 and Eli and Fay around 0.875. Under the model's rules (same window size on both sides), could the two groups ever start influencing each other again?

options.text: No. Each group averages only its own members, so Ann's group can never rise above its own top opinion and Eli's group can never fall below its own bottom one. The gap cannot shrink below ε.
options.feedback: Right. An average never goes past the largest or smallest number in it. With no chain across the split, each side stays boxed in by its own members, so the gap stays wider than ε for good.

options.text: Yes. Everyone keeps averaging, and averaging always pulls opinions together in the end.
options.feedback: That held in the first concept, where everyone listened to everyone. Here averaging only pulls together people inside the same window. Across a split nobody is inside anyone's window, so there is nothing to pull the two groups together.

options.text: Yes, if Ann's group drifts upward far enough to come within ε of Eli.
options.feedback: Ann's group can only average values it already holds, all at or below its current top opinion. Nothing pulls it upward, because the only people above it are out of reach.

options.text: Only if Eli and Fay change their minds first and move down toward Ann's group.
options.feedback: Eli and Fay average only each other, so their opinions stay between their own values and cannot move down past them. Inside this model nobody chooses to change; the rules decide, and they keep the gap open.

hints: Can an average be larger than the largest number you averaged?
What is the highest opinion anyone in Ann's group listens to?

activities.question: The paper also studies windows that reach farther to the right than to the left. Suppose a gap is within one person's longer reach but outside the other person's shorter reach. What does the paper say about such a split?

options.text: It can close again, unlike a split that neither side can see across.
options.feedback: Correct. In a one-sided split one side still listens across the gap and keeps being pulled toward the other side, so the gap can narrow. The paper notes that one-sided splits can close again, while two-sided splits never do.

options.text: It can never close, just like any other split.
options.feedback: The never-close rule depends on nobody on either side listening across the gap. In a one-sided split one side still does, so that guarantee breaks. The paper reports that one-sided splits can close.

options.text: It closes immediately in the next round.
options.feedback: The paper says one-sided splits can close, not that they must, and not straight away. Whether one closes depends on how the opinions keep moving.

hints: The argument for permanence needed both sides to be out of each other's reach.
In a one-sided split, does anyone still listen across the gap?

concepts.title: The edges get pulled in and the middle gets torn apart
concepts.idea: People near the extremes have others on only one side of their window, so they move inward and bunch up, and these bunches then pull nearby opinions away from the centre in opposite directions.

predict.question: New case: everyone starts evenly spread, but only between 0.3 and 0.7, so nobody holds an extreme view. Everyone listens within 0.1 of their own opinion. In the first round, who moves?
options: The people nearest 0.3 and 0.7 move inward; the rest stay put
Nobody moves, because nobody is near 0 or 1
Everyone moves toward 0.5 at the same speed
why: Right. What matters is the edge of where people actually are, not the ends of the scale. Someone at 0.3 finds others only on their right within 0.1, so the average pulls them inward. People deeper inside have balanced windows.
Tempting if you tie the effect to the numbers 0 and 1. But the person at 0.3 has nobody below them, so their window is just as one-sided as it would be at 0.
The centre is actually the last place to feel anything. A person at 0.5 has equal crowds on both sides within 0.1, so their average is their own opinion.
Averaging only moves you when your window is lopsided. Only people within 0.1 of the occupied edges have lopsided windows, so only they move at first.

terms.means: A starting spread where every pair of neighbouring opinions is the same distance apart
When everyone you listen to sits on the same side of you, so averaging can only pull you that way
A crowded spot where many opinions have piled up close together

model.title: How far each person moves in the next round
model.note: Teaching model: an evenly spread population on the 0–1 scale, using the paper's symmetric rule (everyone averages all opinions within ε of their own, all updating at once). The second slider stands in for time passing: it replaces everyone who started within that distance of an edge with one crowd sitting at that distance. This simplifies how real crowds form and keep moving. The flat stretch to the left of the left crowd (and to the right of the right crowd) shows the crowd's own move. Only one round of moves is shown. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: How far the edges have moved in and piled up

outputs.label: Next move of the person at 0.25
outputs.expr: (max(0, min(1 - s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) + eps) - max(s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) - eps)) * (min(1 - s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) + eps) + max(s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) - eps)) / 2 + s * s * (clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) - s <= eps ? 1 : 0) + s * (1 - s) * (1 - s - clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) <= eps ? 1 : 0)) / (max(0, min(1 - s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) + eps) - max(s, clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) - eps)) + s * (clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) - s <= eps ? 1 : 0) + s * (1 - s - clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s) <= eps ? 1 : 0)) - clamp(0.25, s, 1 - s)

outputs.label: Next move of the person at 0.48 (just left of centre)
Next move of the person at 0.52 (just right of centre)

y.label: Move in the next round (up = toward 1)

series.label: Next move now
series.expr: (max(0, min(1 - s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) + eps) - max(s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) - eps)) * (min(1 - s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) + eps) + max(s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) - eps)) / 2 + s * s * (clamp(x, s, 1 - s) - s <= eps ? 1 : 0) + s * (1 - s) * (1 - s - clamp(x, s, 1 - s) <= eps ? 1 : 0)) / (max(0, min(1 - s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) + eps) - max(s, clamp(x, s, 1 - s) - eps)) + s * (clamp(x, s, 1 - s) - s <= eps ? 1 : 0) + s * (1 - s - clamp(x, s, 1 - s) <= eps ? 1 : 0)) - clamp(x, s, 1 - s)

series.label: Next move at the even start
series.expr: (max(0, x - eps) + min(1, x + eps)) / 2 - x

steps.say: Each spot on this solid curve is one person. Across is where their opinion sits now. Up or down is how far it moves next round.
Above this line means moving up toward 1. Below means moving down toward 0. On the line means staying put.
This slider sets ε, how far each person listens. Watch the curve change shape.
This slider lets time pass: the outermost people move inward and pile up at the edges you see marked.
The dashed curve keeps the starting picture, so you can compare.

explore.prompt: Now steer the model yourself: first find out how far the edge pull reaches at the start, then tear the middle apart under new conditions.

goals.text: Before the edges pile up at all, make the person a quarter of the way along start to move.
hints: At the start, who moves at all? Only people whose window spills over an edge of the spread.
Keep the piling-up slider at zero. Ask yourself how wide a window must be for the person at 0.25 to reach past 0.
That person's distance from 0 is the threshold. Go one or two notches past it and watch their point lift off the line.

goals.text: Using a wider listening range than the walkthrough did, tear the middle apart: the person just left of centre moves left and the person just right of centre moves right.
hints: The middle tears when each person beside the centre can reach a different crowd.
A crowd reaches as far as its own position plus the listening range. Widen the range first, then move the crowds.
Slide the crowds in until the left crowd's reach ends right around the centre. With a wider range, they need to march in less far than before.

feedback.correct: Yes. The pull comes from lopsided windows, and windows are lopsided at the edges of wherever people actually are. With everyone between 0.3 and 0.7, the people at 0.3 and 0.7 have company on one side only, so they move inward first, and the change works toward the centre from there.
feedback.incorrect: You may have tied the effect to the ends of the scale, or to the centre. The rule only moves someone when the people within their range are not balanced around them. Inside an even crowd, windows are balanced. At the edges of the crowd, wherever those edges are, they are not.

steps.say: Start with everyone spread evenly from 0 to 1, each listening within 0.2. Neighbours all sit the same distance apart. The paper calls this a regular start profile.

Look at the person at 0. Everyone in their window, from 0 to 0.2, is on their right. The average is 0.1, so they jump up by 0.1. This is one-sided influence: nobody sits on the other side to pull back.
From 0.2 to 0.8 the curve sits flat on the line. Each of these people has an equal crowd on both sides, so their average is their own opinion. The middle does not move yet.
Widen the range to 0.3. Now the edge pull reaches 0.3 in from each side, and the quiet middle shrinks.
Back to 0.2, and let time pass. Everyone who started within 0.15 of an edge has piled into one crowd at 0.15 (and at 0.85). A crowded spot like this is a condensed region.

See the dip just inside the crowd's reach. People about 0.1 to 0.2 away from the crowd now move down, toward it. That is away from the centre. The crowd pulls in thinly populated opinions within its range.

Let the crowds march further in, to 0.3 and 0.7. Their reach now ends right at the centre. The person just left of centre can reach only the left crowd, and the person just right can reach only the right crowd.
So the middle is torn: one side is yanked down and the other yanked up, by the biggest moves on the screen. Soon a gap wider than 0.2 opens there, a split that, as you saw earlier, never heals.

understand.explanation: People near the edges of the spread find others only on their inner side, so averaging pushes them inward, while people in the middle have balanced windows and stay put. As the edges move in, they pile up into crowds. A crowd pulls everyone within its reach toward itself, and near the centre that means pulling outward. When the crowds' reach meets in the middle, the person just left of centre is dragged left and the one just right is dragged right, so the middle tears and a split opens. The paper traced this in a run with 50 evenly spaced opinions and ε = 0.2 (Figures 4 and 5): changes start at the edges, reach the centre last with the biggest jumps, and the profile splits in period 6. With random starting opinions, chance crowding creates extra crowds and splits inside the population from the very first round. These are simulation results for one simple rule, not measurements of real groups.
understand.quote: In the symmetric case the major causes for polarisation are splits in the opinion profiles. They are caused by shrinking and condensing at the extremes, condensing induced by condensing, and condensing induced by density fluctuations in randomly generated start profiles.

check.task: Keep the edges piled up into crowds, but make those crowds pull the people beside the centre toward the centre instead of tearing them apart.
check.hint: The tearing happened because each person beside the centre could reach only one crowd. What changes if they can reach both crowds at once?
check.misconception: That crowds always tear the middle apart. A crowd pulls whoever is within its reach toward itself. A person beside the centre who can reach both equal crowds is pulled toward their midpoint, which is the centre.

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence rule (BC) with one shared confidence level. Each person's next opinion is the plain average of everyone within ε of them, including themselves. The coloured ε is the listening-range slider. The curve plots this average minus the person's current opinion. A crowd simply counts as many people j sitting at the same spot, which is why it pulls so hard on the average.

concepts.recap: People at the edges feel pull from only one side, so they move inward and pile up; those crowds then drag nearby opinions toward themselves, tearing the middle in two.

activities.prompt: Follow the paper's own run (Figures 4 and 5): 50 evenly spaced opinions, everyone listening within 0.2, all updating at the same time.

stages.label: Round 0: even spacing
stages.text: Every opinion is within 0.2 of its neighbours, so the whole population is one connected chain of people who listen to each other.

stages.label: The edges move in
stages.text: The most extreme opinions feel pull from only one side and move toward the centre, so the range of opinions shrinks. From round 0 to 1, nothing in the middle changes.

stages.label: The edges pile up
stages.text: Near each end, opinions bunch together into dense crowds.

stages.label: Crowds recruit their neighbours
stages.text: Each crowd attracts opinions from thinner areas within its reach. Round by round the changes work inward toward the centre.

stages.label: The centre is torn
stages.text: In the centre, opinions above 0.5 move up and those below 0.5 move down. The centre opinions are the last to be affected, and they make the biggest jumps.

stages.label: The split
stages.text: In round 6 the chain breaks. From then on the two halves are separate communities that no longer interact, and from round 7 to 8 onwards nothing changes at all.

activities.takeaway: Two camps come from a chain of events: one-sided pull at the edges, piling up, crowds recruiting inward, and finally a tear in the middle. The paper notes that a random start works the same way, plus chance crowding that triggers extra splits from the start.

concepts.title: Many opinions, then two camps, then consensus
concepts.idea: As the confidence level ε grows, a population passes through sharp phases: many surviving opinions at small ε, two camps at medium ε, and one consensus at large ε.

predict.question: Take a range that split the full crowd (opinions spread from 0 to 1) into two camps. Keep that exact range, but start a new crowd whose opinions only spread from 0.2 to 0.8. What is the most likely end?
options: Still two camps, just a little closer together
why: This is tempting if you think the range alone decides the outcome. What matters is the range compared with how spread out the crowd is. In a crowd only 0.6 wide, the same range acts like a much wider one on the full scale, which falls in the agreement phase.

Correct. The rule only uses distances and averages, so squeezing the crowd is the same as widening the range. A two-camp range divided by 0.6 lands in the consensus phase, so the edges are pulled together before a gap can open.
Many groups come from a range that is small compared with the crowd's width. Here the range is relatively larger, not smaller, so you get fewer groups.
Each person still has others within their range, so averaging still moves them. Only a range far smaller than the gaps between people would freeze everyone.

terms.means: The paper's name for the outcome where many different opinions survive at the end
Here: the crowd ends in two separate camps, one on each side, with an empty middle
A stretch of settings that all give the same kind of outcome, with sudden switches between stretches

model.title: A whole crowd averaging with the people in range, from a random start
model.note: Teaching model: runs the paper's bounded-confidence rule (Hegselmann–Krause: everyone updates at once to the average of all opinions within ε of their own, one equal range for all). It uses 200 people with random starting opinions on a 0–1 scale, not the paper's 625. Groups are counted as clumps separated by gaps wider than 0.1. At very small ranges the surviving opinions sit closer than that, so the counter merges neighbours and reads too low. With so few people, a tiny leftover group sometimes lingers between two camps. The exact switch points shift with crowd size and the random start. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Gap between the two most extreme people

steps.say: Each dot is one person, holding an opinion somewhere between 0 and 1. They start scattered at random.
Every round, everyone at once moves to the average of the opinions within their listening range. The run plays on until opinions stop moving.
This slider sets the listening range ε: how far away an opinion can be and still be heard.
This box counts the separate groups left at the end.
This one shows how far apart the two most extreme people end up.
And this slider swaps in a different random starting crowd.

explore.prompt: You start in the many-groups setting with crowd 1. Move the listening range to find the other two kinds of outcome.

goals.text: Get crowd 1 to settle into exactly two camps with an empty middle
hints: From the many-groups start, should the range get narrower or wider?
Widen it a little at a time and watch the group counter. Stop before everyone merges into one.
Two camps live in a fairly narrow band below a quarter of the scale. Edge up slowly from where you are.

goals.text: Bring the whole of crowd 1 to one shared opinion while each person still ignores anyone more than a third of the scale away
hints: What does a wider range do to the gap between the most extreme people?
Go wider than the two-camp band until the gap box drops to nearly zero, but stay under the goal's limit.
Agreement arrives well before people listen to the whole scale. Look just below the limit.

feedback.correct: Right. The outcome depends on the range compared with how wide the crowd is. A crowd squeezed into 0.6 of the scale behaves like the full crowd with a range about 1.7 times wider, and that lands in the consensus phase.
feedback.incorrect: You probably treated the range as if it decided the outcome alone. The averaging rule only looks at distances, so a narrower crowd with the same range is the same as the full crowd with a wider range. That moves it from the two-camp phase into the agreement phase.

steps.say: Walk the range from narrow to wide on crowd 2. A tiny range first: people hear only near neighbours, so many small clumps survive. The paper calls this plurality. (The counter undercounts here.)
Widen it: the clumps merge into fewer, bigger groups, but they still stretch from edge to edge.
Wider again, and the picture snaps into a new pattern: two big camps, one on each side, with the middle emptied out. This is polarisation in the paper's sense.
Keep widening and it snaps once more: one group near the middle, and the gap between the most extreme people shrinks to almost nothing. Consensus.
These three outcomes are phases: whole stretches of ranges give the same kind of result, with sudden jumps between them rather than a smooth slide.
Now go back to the middle. Making everyone more open-minded did not bring the crowd steadily closer to agreement. At medium range it reliably split in two.
Why? Edge people hear others only on their inner side, so they move inward and bunch up. The bunches pull the middle apart in opposite directions, and once a gap exceeds the range it never closes.

understand.explanation: As the listening range ε widens, the end result does not change smoothly. It jumps between three phases: many surviving opinions (plurality), two camps (polarisation), then one consensus. The paper showed this by running 625 randomly placed opinions, all updating at once. It stepped ε from 0.01 to 0.4 in 40 steps and repeated each step 50 times with fresh random starts. With ε = 0.01, 38 opinions survived. With ε = 0.15 the agents ended in two camps, and with ε = 0.25 everyone agreed. Above 0.4 the result was always consensus. The middle phase is the surprise, and the earlier ideas explain it: the edges are pulled only inward, bunch up and drag the middle apart, and gaps wider than ε are permanent. Caveats: this is a model in which everyone can hear everyone within range and all ranges are equal, and the exact switch points depend on the start. The authors' first simulations with only local neighbours suggest the two-camp phase can disappear there.
understand.quote: Summing up and generalising what we see in Figure 3 one might say: As the homogeneous and symmetric confidence interval increases we transit from phase to phase. More exactly, we step from fragmentation (plurality) over polarisation (polarity) to consensus (conformity).

check.task: Show that the split is not a fluke of one start. Choose a starting crowd numbered 3 or higher and get it to end in two big camps far apart. A tiny leftover group between them is allowed.
check.hint: Change the crowd slider first. Then search the middle band of ranges, between many groups and agreement, until two or three groups remain and the extreme people are still far apart.
check.misconception: That the two camps came from one lucky random start, rather than being the typical outcome at medium range (the paper found it across 50 random starts per setting).

connect.caption: This is the paper's bounded-confidence model (BC), the rule the simulation runs. Each person i moves to the plain average of everyone j whose opinion lies within ε of their own; I(i, x) is that set of people. The coloured ε is the listening-range slider. Sweeping it is the paper's walk along the diagonal, and the group counter shows which phase you land in.

concepts.recap: Widening the listening range moves a crowd through sharp phases: many groups, then two camps, then one. So more open-mindedness can split a group before it unites it.
